utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We will go into closed session for the witness to come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness arrives, Your Honour, I would like to point out one problem. At the very outset of this trial regarding statements admitted under 92 ter, the Trial Chamber decided that those statements on the notification list are statements that go under 92 ter, and on that basis the Defence prepares for its cross-examination. I now find out that the Milutinovic transcript, both redacted and unredacted, has not been exhibited; and we prepared our entire cross-examination based on it, that is not to cover again the issues, the questions, covered in the Milutinovic transcript. And let me point out immediately the statement 2668 refers to the Milutinovic transcript, both unredacted and redacted, as we find it in the notification. And as to the facts covered by this transcript, if we included them in our cross-examination, it would be much, much longer. The Defence relied on what we thought had been agreed. We did not want to introduce issues that were on the 92 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is correct we had originally listed the transcript, but we decided not to tender it. I have informed my colleague that if he seeks to tender the transcript that is not a problem. We had prepared a public, redacted, version of the transcript which is also in e-court, and the 65 ter numbers have been indicated in the notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that may have overcome the issue with this witness, but I have a recollection that this issue may have gone unnoticed with some previous witnesses because not always, I think, has every statement or every transcript been tendered. What concerns me is the original decision of the Chamber about admission and about the expectation of the parties with respect to all the transcripts and statements that were dealt with in that original decision. It was certainly the expectation of the Chamber that those statements and transcripts which had identified as properly admissible would in due course be tendered. The problem may only be with this witness, but I suspect that there are some other witnesses similarly affected. I think we will need to look at that - not right now - and it may be that there will need to be some regularisation, that is, a tendering of things that may have been omitted. I think it's fair to say that there was an expectation which probably was shared by the Defence but certainly of the Chamber that we would have all of these documents tendered in due course. And it would be dangerous to leave that matter not properly considered at the point of receiving exhibits in case it is the situation that something was omitted which the Defence thought was going to be tendered, something was omitted from the tendering. In the present case for this present witness, I'm sure Mr. Djurdjic will take up your offer of tendering the transcript that was not tendered by you. But we will have a look at other witnesses to see whether there has been a due tendering of the statements. And perhaps you might convey to Mr. Stamp our view that in future -- for future witnesses if there is not to be a tendering of each of the statements and transcripts which we had identified in our primary decision or decisions, that it should be specifically mentioned in court that even though the Prosecution had originally proposed the tendering, it does not now seek to tender. If that is done, the Chamber can consider and the Defence can consider whether there is a concern about the Prosecution not proceeding as originally proposed where its tender of all statements and transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may address the matter just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I remember that a couple months ago when this came up I was in court and I had to address it. The practice so far since this issue was first raised by the Defence has always been that we notified them when we do not seek to tender everything that was listed in the third column of our annexes to the motion. That has been the practice so far. In this case it was simply an oversight from our part not to notify them - and it's actually my oversight; we should have e-mailed them - but the practice so far had been that. So we have each time always informed the Defence. If we listed more material than we intend to tender, we always let them know beforehand whenever we send out the notification; so so far this has always been done, and it has been done by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, no need to deal with the matter further now unless you have been able to consider it, but is it the case that so far you've been satisfied wherever the Prosecution has not formally tendered a statement or a transcript of one of the earlier witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think you stated the practice so far the most precisely. The Defence had raised that issue in the past, and you said everything will be admitted that the Prosecution offers for admission and that's how the Defence will prepare, and that's how we did so far. Here we have the list again. If something was not on the list, the Defence never thought we should put it in. You put it very well today, and I would suggest immediately that these two exhibits, 05203 and 05203.01, the redacted and unredacted transcripts, be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They certainly will be received, Mr. Djurdjic, and we understand from what you have said that the Defence has no concern or objection in respect of any earlier witness so far in the trial, that there has been a failure to tender either a statement or a transcript of that witness which the Defence had wanted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The invaluable [Realtime transcript read in error "infallible"] Marie O'Leary again brought this situation to my notice earlier today. I always relied on the supposition that whatever is on the list will be tendered, but I cannot really say anything until my assistant checks whether we have admitted all this evidence so far or not. I promise that within a few days, probably sooner, because Ms. O'Leary is very efficient, we will submit to the Court everything that is on the list and has not yet been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, then we will leave this issue open, as my earlier comments indicated, to enable you to consider whether there is something that has been unwittingly omitted. And I'm not sure whether line 24 correctly records what you said, was it infallible or invaluable?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. I will make an order for all of this to be recorded in public session. We had gone into closed session, but it will be recorded in open session because it is of procedural significance.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in public session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. We left off yesterday on the issue of your departure on the 25th. Were you in the motorcade, the column of vehicles that started from Prizren to Trnje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How many vehicles were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, around five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one small vehicle that we called Pinzgauer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I suppose there was someone in the cab with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And in that motorcade, your truck was which number in the line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second in the line, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And who was driving ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did that vehicle lead the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You as a driver, before you went out into the field on the 25th, did you have a meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How did you know where to drive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that first truck, there must have been one of the NCOs and the NCOs did attend a meeting because it was late at night that these meetings were usually held.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: As you went by certain places, there were boards and traffic signs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, before the war there were normal traffic signs in the whole Prizren area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must not have been paying attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And from June 1998 you served in Prizren and the Prizren area as a driver. You must have paid attention to the roads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but when you are in a motorcade, you don't need to pay attention, you just follow the car ahead of you, and you don't pay attention to the signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you got out of the trucks in the place you -- where you stopped, how many troops were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those two or three lorries that were there were full, and I drove a lorry full of food. I was not able to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But occasionally you would drive troops as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was the type of that lorry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dietz [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How many troops fit in a Dietz lorry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there were three lorries full of troops, how many could there have been in -- maximum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not really packed if you really want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how about the Pinzgauer, who was in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I remember in the military police there is a space behind the cab for troops. Is that the kind you had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So who was there behind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three soldiers and the commander drove.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And who was in the cab with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: At what time did you leave Prizren?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After midnight, late.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And when did you arrive at destination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early in the morning. It was still dark; I remember that. And the time it took us to find our positions -- I think it was about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when you arrived at destination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was it night or day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And now tell me, we finished yesterday with those teams, and you seem to have said there were two teams?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were more, but two teams left first, followed by another two teams, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you explain a bit more, how was this redistribution done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they would discuss it with the commander, I mean the NCOs would discuss it with the commander, and then they would pass it on. And every NCO chose which soldiers he would pick.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you in that food lorry when you came to the destination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And where was the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We've talked so far and you didn't mention a single commander except that one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you don't stand in one place, you move all the time. Sometimes you take over. The commander doesn't stand still. He also has to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you please take care to tell me only what you know from seeing it with your own eyes. Don't tell me what happens in theory or what should happen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was late, it was still dark. I didn't see much of him anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I agree that you can't remember the details, but when you talk about whatever, please tell me only what you saw. We've now been talking for now five, perhaps ten minutes. You didn't see a single commanding officer except that battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe there was one commanding officer with me. I think that one -- let me not mention him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You told me you drove food supplies. How many teams did you make?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, reckon that there was one team per truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So to which team were you attached?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of those teams. I can't remember exactly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you see? And if we zoom out would that be better?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you put a circle around Mamusa.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that would be roughly that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I can see quite well on this map. Put a number 1, please, to the left of the circle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you please mark Medvedce village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll put a dot here. I think it's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Trnje village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I asked you about Medvedce.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see well enough here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Put number 2 next to Trnje.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And below, circle number one. Do you see the name Medvedce just below the circle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's it. Can you put number 3 there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And now tell me, 1 is Mamusa, 2 is Trnje, and 3 is Medvedce. Relative to Mamusa, where is Medvedce? I mean north? South? East? West?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This seems to be south-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about Trnje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In your statement given in April, paragraph 2, page 6; in English that's page 5, paragraph 4, you say: "We participated in the encircling of the area near Mamusa. My unit had a position in one Albanian village just south of Mamusa." Now, tell me, which village is south of Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps when I was giving the statement I said roughly speaking because we located things together with the investigator, we located our area, and he -- and I -- I'll draw a line her, that's our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And when did you do that with the investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the 28th of July or June when we went there photographing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I think the village was Medvedce.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is what you said in the first statement true? I'll quote it exactly. That's the statement given 25th and 26th of April, 2002. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now tender this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned D00115, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I asked you a question yesterday and on transcript 4389, lines 9 through 19, you told me that the soldier who told you about this who comes from the same area as you was in the border area, at a border crossing. That was his position; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up P5203 -- sorry, D00013 [sic], that is a triple zero, 13. Page 10.615.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We're waiting for this exhibit to come up. I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, before I begin the question, we admitted this Defence exhibit earlier today, that's Milutinovic transcript D00013 [sic], I think. That was the number given to this exhibit. I'm afraid I was the one who took that down, not Mrs. O'Leary.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's D00113, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever I do, I do wrong it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, and I gave a reference, that this soldier who told you that story was at the border crossing. Here we have the document on the screen. In the Milutinovic trial in response to a direct question, Did this soldier who told you this tell you that he was at the border crossing as a soldier, you said no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this. Yesterday I said he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's move on. I want one thing cleared up regarding Jeskovo. Hamit Thaqi, Hunjen Rexhepi, Bashkim Supa, Hajdar Shalja, Feriz Susuri, Tahir Gashi, Skender Latifi, Umredin Chengaj, Aledin Dzezahiri, soldiers of the special unit of the 125th Brigade Operation Zone Pastrik died a heros' death in Jeskovo. What I read to you is from "The Road to Freedom" by Zafir Berisha, commander of that brigade. You were there. Did you see any bodies of KLA members in Jeskovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see the KLA. I'm not sure. There were people in civilian clothes. If they had been wearing uniform, I would have thought they were KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday during the first part of my examination when you told us about various statements and how you gave them, you told me you had lost your passport.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the passport. Telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you never lost your passport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I must have gotten this wrong.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was that about the telephone number? Were you going to Sarajevo to give a statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Sarajevo to the field office of the ICTY to bring my passport to get a visa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's what must have confused me. After the war, were you again in touch with anyone who served in your unit during the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me whether I was in contact with anyone after the war. I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And did you talk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did that person hide at your place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I won't name the person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can say K41.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Okay, K41. I won't say the name of the town. You were not in contact with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was he present --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would request that we go into private session if my learned colleague is going to be asking questions about this protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps as a precaution we could do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see my learned colleague on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I was talking to Ms. O'Leary. I'm sorry for interrupting you. That map that the witness marked, has it been admitted? I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe so, Exhibit D115. Carry on, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have this map up on the screen, and could we please zoom where -- the section where -- that has been marked by the witness. If we could zoom in a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked a series of questions about the action that you participated in the village of Trnje. You have drawn a line across -- between positions numbers 2 and 3 on the map. What does that line represent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That line represents where my unit was deployed, where it had its positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you had initially said that this action was carried out in the village of Medvedce. In July when you visited the area with an investigator from the Office of the Prosecution, did you correct this, the name of the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having visited the area to the best of your recollection where did this action take place, in which village, the action you describe in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In village Trnje, number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you were asked a series of questions by my learned colleague about how you got to the village. Just very roughly speaking, are you able to draw on this map and indicate the direction in which you were advancing, your units were advancing, when you were heading towards the village of Trnje prior to this action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record, the witness has drawn a line with an arrow that goes from the south towards the north and ends at number 2 that has been circled as the village of Trnje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You were also asked about the village of Novaki. Do you see that on the map? I know the map is a bit blurry because it has been zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The witness has drawn a rectangular -- rectangle around the village of Novaki.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked yesterday by my colleague - and this is at page 4414 and 4415 - whether you saw MUP units when you entered the village and you said: "I did not see MUP units on that occasion, but they were there in these days." Were MUP units involved in the action against the village of Trnje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have shown on the map the road your unit took when you were advancing towards this village. Did the MUP units that were involved in this area, did they advance with you along this same road, or were they progressing or coming from a different direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, the witness has drawn a second line to indicate the direction in which MUP units were advancing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you maybe mark that with --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And has marked it as MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know what type of units, MUP units, were involved in this action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the witness has marked the first line that shows the road taken by his units with a VJ.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did the MUP units that were involved in this action, did they -- what was their role? Did they perform similar tasks as the VJ units, or did they have a different task to perform during the conduct of this action against the village of Trnje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a different assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you explain if you know what was their assignment? What were they supposed to do during the course of this action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know; I'm not really sure. But they were probably the first to start implementing that action.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say they were probably the first to start implementing the action, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really wouldn't want to interrupt or to influence, and now I don't know how to express myself without doing either --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let him continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Kravetz, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if these units entered the village of Trnje?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean the MUP units?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the MUP units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was asking about the MUP units. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the course of the following days, I saw MUP members here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, the witness has drawn an arrow above number 2 which he has marked as MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, this first line that you drew alongside the line that is marked VJ, were these units that were moving along that line, that is, from south to north, towards the village of Trnje, were they advancing at the same time as your units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was there any sort of communication between those units, the MUP units and your unit, when this action was being carried out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What sort of communication? I mean, how would you know what sort of progress the MUP units were making along the axis that they were travelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you said that there was sort of communication between MUP and VJ units, what were you referring to? How would you communicate with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the communication was between our officers and them, by radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you said that you saw MUP units in -- along a second axis which you've drawn above number 2. When did you see those MUP units there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that through binoculars. I wasn't right there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where were you when you saw those units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In village Trnje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by my learned colleague - and this is again the same page I had referred to earlier - to clarify whether these units were present when you entered the village and you say -- you said: "No, they were not there on the first day." Did you see them on any of the following days in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what were these units doing in the village when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did the same thing we did. They were waiting, and they must have been involved in an operation before that or -- I really am not sure what to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence which has been marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00785, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just a final clarification before we move away from -- on from this topic. When I asked you what you saw them doing you said: "They did the same thing we did." What did you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Waiting to withdraw from that area. I don't know because the operation was over, and they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see my learned colleague on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say now that he has already -- he has confirmed an answer to the question that he had already given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'll move on from there. If we can have -- I see the map has disappeared at least from -- the map's still there. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The map that was just tendered, I just wanted to ask a final question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, on the map you were asked to mark the village of Mamusa. Do you know what was the ethnicity of the inhabitants of the village of Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Turks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did your VJ unit conduct any actions against that village during the course of this operation that you've drawn there, did you go into the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did later, but the army did not take part in carrying out any action, neither did the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you were asked several questions by my learned colleague about looting and specifically about how you were able to tell which villages were Albanian and which were non-Albanian. And you were asked whether in this area there was a single name of an Albanian village and you said that between the road from Prizren to Djakovica on the left side there was not a single Serbian village and on the road to Prizren there were several Serbian villages, Bosniak villages, and some Albanian villages. Now, with respect to looting of houses, do you recall whether your unit or other VJ units conducted any looting of houses in non-Albanian villages during the time you were deployed in this area of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no looting in the predominantly Serbian villages; however, I think that some Bosnian houses were plundered and the looting was conducted in Albanian houses for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the reference I was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Oh, I see my learned colleague. Just to give the transcript reference I was referring to at page 4421 of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for the witness to finish his answer. Several questions were asked in terms of the ethnicity of the owners of looted houses. My question was: How were they able to distinguish the ethnicity of the owners of the houses. How did they know the houses belonged to Albanians and not to someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That was one of the questions, but the question I mentioned was also asked yesterday. Your Honours, I don't know if this is a convenient time for the break because I have a couple more questions. I think I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you would like to think about that over the break then, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will go into closed session so that the witness can leave.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'll just wait for a second while the blinds come up. Sir, yesterday you were asked a series of questions about the action you participated in Jeskovo or Jeskovo and you were -- my learned colleague from the Defence read out some passages from two reports of -- by the OSCE and my learned colleague - and this is at page 4437 - asked you after reading the passage: "You see that the monitors knew that the KLA was present in Jeskovo?" And you said: "I understand this but why did they prevent them from coming any closer to the road." My learned colleague asked: So you knew they were all the time? "Yes they were seen." What were you referring to when you said: Why did they prevent them from coming to the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OSCE was prevented to come closer to that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Prevented by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said yesterday that - and this was at page 4438 - that -- my learned colleague read a passage of a report and said: "On the second day they went out to make an inspection if that's what you would call it." And you said: "And what about the first day. Where were they?" And my learned colleague said: "But they were at the entrance as you could hear." And you said: "The operation was completed before the night." Do you know whether the OSCE representatives were allowed into the village once the action was completed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not allowed to enter the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that you and your unit entered the village and you mentioned seeing bodies there and my learned colleague asked you some questions about that. Were any of the bodies that you saw in Jeskovo after this operation was completed, were any of them in KLA uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: While you were in the village, did you see any signs of KLA presence in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K54 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I noticed bunkers and sandbags, probably they were there. That's the only thing that I noticed though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know that completes the questioning for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming again to The Hague and for the assistance you've been able to give, and you may now return to your normal activities. We will go into closed session again to enable you to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The next upcoming witness is Mr. Qamil Shabani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: He will testify pursuant to 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will say the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Ms. Nilsen has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: My name is Qamil Shabani.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I was born on the -- on the 14th of the 11th, 1952, in Zhegra.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Zegra, is that a village in Gjilan municipality?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, it's a village in Gjilan municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And are you still living in this village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, I continue to live there. That's where I was living, and I'm still living in the same village.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: What is your profession, Mr. Shabani?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I was a teacher, but it's some time that I'm not exercising this profession. I am privately employed, self-employed on family matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And are you educated as a teacher?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I was qualified and graduated in the Faculty of Technology, and I worked as a teacher from 1974 until the 21st -- in fact, up until 2001 in an elementary school and then in the gymnasium of Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Shabani, did you provide a statement to the Office of Prosecution in June 2001?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, I made a statement in June 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And did you in August 2006 provide additional information and give an amended version of your statement to the Office of Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. I made additional information available so that it's -- so that we have clearer information about the events in my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Right. Did you have a chance to read through those statements before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity to read them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the information contained in these statements from 2001 and 2006 is true and accurate and -- to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, as far as I'm aware and as far as I believe, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender those two statements into evidence, two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter number for the 2001 statement is 02263.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00786, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And 2006 statement has 65 ter number 02280.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00787.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Did you also testify, Mr. Shabani, on the 31st of August and the 1st of September, 2006, in the Milutinovic et al. case for this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: All right. Have you been given also a chance to review this transcript together with a language assistant before you came to court today?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity to look at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If I asked you the same questions as you were asked in 2006, would you then provide me with the same answer?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, I will try and provide the same answers that I gave then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I seek to tender the transcript into evidence with 65 ter number 05071, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00788, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: There are also two associated exhibits for this 92 bis witness. The first is an exhibit containing different examples of vehicles, and the second is an exhibit containing different examples of uniforms used by the Serb forces. They have already been tendered and received, and they have been given number P00318 and Exhibit P00325 this is only for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I would now like to read out the court summary for this witness, and after that I will have a few questions. The witness has described that two or three weeks before the air-strikes started Serb army and paramilitary managed to create a check-point on the edge of the village of Zegra with 15 to 20 soldiers. The witness describes their uniforms and their weapons. Initially Serb forces occupied a local house and transformed it into a base for 70 to 80 soldiers. When the air-strikes started, five additional Albanian houses in the village were occupied and the owners were forced out. On the 28th of March, 1999, Serb forces searched for prominent people in the village and shot the LDK, that is, Democratic League of Kosovo, president's brother, and injured his sister. The next morning, on the 29th of March, 1999, the Serb forces started to expel people from their houses, ordering them to leave the village, and threaten them with their weapons. The witness left the village that day together with his family and 1300 other people and went approximately 10 kilometres outside the village towards Donja Stubla, which is Vitina municipality, and they spent the night outside there. The following morning they returned back to the village Zegra, but because the armed vehicles drove through the village firing with machine-guns, they escaped once again and this time they went to the village Donja Stubla. Approximately one week after, Serb forces started to attack the surrounding villages of Donja Stubla, resulting in wounding of women and children and six people were killed. This also resulted in the presence of up to 20.000 displaced people in this little village of Donja Stubla. The witness and his family stayed in Donja Stubla for approximately five weeks. On the 2nd of May they left with a group of 600 people for Macedonia. The following morning they continued to an area in Gjilan municipality called Rustaj where they were surrounded by forces and detained for two hours. The men were separated from the women and the group was threatened with weapons. They were then escorted by 30 to 40 paramilitaries to a hill near the Macedonian border from where the witness was interrogated. Finally the witness was allowed to continue to the border into Macedonia. This is the end of the court summary. If we could please have up 65 ter number 00036 on the screen, please. And if the usher could assist the witness with a pen because I would like him to mark something on it. If we could zoom it in a little bit more, the area to the right side, lower right side of the map. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, are you able to locate on this map your village where you were from, Zegra?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Good. Could you please mark it with a circle and put a 1 next to it.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. We know from your statements and your previous testimony that you escaped to a village not far away and stayed there for five weeks. Could you please put a circle around this place, this village, and then mark a number 2 next to it.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And this place would be -- the name of this village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Lower Stublla.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Or Donja Stubla in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Or Donja Stubla.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the date that you arrived Donja Stubla and the day you left this village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. On the 30th of March we arrived in Upper Stublla. On the 2nd of May, we started leaving Lower Stublla, which means we stayed there around five weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Exactly. And from Donja Stubla we know from your previous statements and testimony that you fled to the Macedonian border. Can you just explain to us why you decided to leave Donja Stubla after five weeks?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. We were not -- we did not feel safe in Lower Stublla. We didn't feel safe because in the surrounding areas there were Serb forces, and we feared that they would come to us and provoke a massacre. And our food supplies were running out so there was uncertainty, and due to this uncertainty we decided to leave towards Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. On your way to the Macedonian border, you reached a place called Rustaj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Good. And do you remember when you reached this place?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: We arrived there. We stayed a night in the hills of Seferaj village, and the following day we went to Rustaj. That's where we came across military and paramilitary Serb forces around 2.00 after midday. That's where they received us and all the column of people was taken, the people were searched, and we waited for a couple of hours for the commander of that unit operating in that area until he arrived. And when he arrived, the operation to search every single individual, male and female, and then they separated the male population from the female. They forced us men to get together at one point and we were encircled by Serb soldiers and paramilitary who were threatening us with their weapons. We feared that we'd be liquidated. There was a heavy rain at that time, and we could hear the voices from our wives and mothers and children who were fearing for our lives. So after some time, Serb forces then brought us together, both groups, and they were escorting us. It was about 70 soldiers and paramilitary, together with their commander they escorted us to a valley, to a meadow - let's call it a meadow --

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to stop you there. Could you just explain whether anything concrete happened to you in this place that you call Rustaj?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, more specifically, when we went to that meadow, the commander of that region together with three or four paramilitaries who were armed, they got closer to me and they said, You, Professor, they spoke in Serbo-Croat, who is the organiser, the leader of this march? And then there was a conversation for about an hour. There were threats and insults against me and my ethnic group. I thought that following this threat they would lead me away and kill me, but that didn't happen. Fortunately that didn't happen because I was -- I kept my cool in the face of the provocations.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to locate this place, Rustaj, on the map; and if you are, could you please put a circle around it and a number 3 next to it. You can also draw a line between number 2 and 3 like you have done with number 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. This is sufficient. Are you also able to see on the map where you crossed the border to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. These are the Lojane mountains. This is the border with Serbia. This is direction towards Rusheva [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. That's the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And this is the place you call Lojane; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, the mountain, the mountains of Lojane, belonging to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Shabani.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00789, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I have no further questions with this witness at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Shabani. My name is Veljko Djurdjic. I'm a member of the Defence team for the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic, assisted by Ms. Marie O'Leary, also a member of our Defence team. I hope we will communicate well and allow the interpreters to do their job. Therefore, when you see the typing finish on the screen, only then start your answer, and I will do the same. Mr. Shabani, what is your occupation now?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I work in agriculture, work in my land. I'm also a handy craftsman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are you perhaps retired?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the structure of the Zegra village in terms of educational attainment and training?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Educational structure and training structure in Zhegra, I'm not clear about this question. I don't know what you want me to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: First of all you started answering and then you said you didn't understand. What I meant is, What level of education did the greatest part of the village reach? Primary school or high school? That was my first question. And my second question was to be: What is the occupation of most of the village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: There are people with university education, there are people who have got secondary education, and there are people who have only been to the elementary school. As for the schools that exist in our village, we've got an elementary school and a gymnasium, and it's got its parallel structures in Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean to ask about schooling institutions. Do you know perhaps which percentage of the village population only finished primary school?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I'm not into statistics, but I could say most of them have been through the elementary school, most of them, most of the village population with percentage terms I could say 60, 70 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps I was not precise enough. My main question related to 1999. All my questions will be mainly about 1999, and if I want to ask something about a different period, I will indicate so. This percentage you gave me, it refers to 1999?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's related to that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that over 40 per cent of the population has more than primarily school, for instance, finished secondary school or higher, university, for instance?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, that's roughly the case. I do not know exactly what the statistics are because I haven't been involved with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in terms of occupation, what would you say is the occupation of the majority of the villages of Zegrani?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: At that time, that is, in 1999 and before then, most of them were involved in agriculture or in various crafts or they were employed by schools, some worked in factories in Gjilan and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll explain why I asked this. Most of the witnesses we have seen so far were teachers or people with university degrees and most of the witnesses are people who live outside of big cities, that's why I asked. And now, tell me, in 1999 who were you living with?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I lived with my wife in Zhegra.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I read that in the statement. I meant did you live with your parents, your brothers, in one household?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: No. We had separate houses, four brothers, one has passed away. And I've talked about that in my statements during the Milosevic case. Three of us are still alive, and we live in separate houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does your family house have a yard?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is the yard surrounded by a wall?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Partly, just a small part of it, and another part has got other objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That part with a wall, where was the wall built and how tall is it?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: There is a barn there which we have built. That's -- that's a wall -- it's a building, it's a building, which serves a purpose in my family's interest in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How high is that building?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: It's a one-storey building, and it stretches several metres long, and there is part of the building where we store the fodder and part of it it's where the animals live.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that structure separate your house from the street or the yard from the street?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, this building separates my proper house from the road, so this is on the side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is there a gate leading to the yard?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How high is the gate?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The gate is about 2 metres high, and there is another gate where the cards [as interpreted] go in and it's like 3, 4 metres high and long.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters say cars rather than cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What is the gate made of?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Concrete blocks and wood. The groundwork, it's made of stones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How large is your own plot of land?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I have some 2 and a half hectares, and it's on the plain and on the hill-sides including.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, in your statement I read that in 1978 you did your military service in the town of Vranje. What was your military specialty?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Not in Vranje but in Kranj in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the interpreters misunderstood me. I said Kranj. My question was: What was your military specialty?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: It was pyro-ing [as interpreted] engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now when we're talking about 1999, when was your memory of it the best?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I can't understand the way you formulate this question. I do not see -- I can't make sense, what's the aim of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I mean that you have given quite a few statements and you testified on several occasions in court; and when we're now talking about events from 1999, when was your recollection of these events the best?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: My memory is quite clear now, and it was quite clear then when -- when it -- when we talk about events that I have been through.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I noted down that I wanted to show to you a couple of discrepancies compared to your first statement, it's P786. Earlier today in line 46 -- line -- on page 46 of the transcript of the LiveNote you described how you came to the border crossing of Rustaj. And you said you were searched, mistreated, and so on. Could you tell me again what was the first thing that happened when you came to Rustaj? Who did what to you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Are you talking about Rustaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: We were surrounded by the forces. We had to wait for a couple of hours and then there was a detailed search of each individual in the convoy, men or women, young or old. After the detailed search, they separated men from the women. We were encircled, and we were being threatened with automatic rifles, and that to us was a signal that we were going to be killed. And we feared that we would be executed at any moment then, but that didn't happen. And when we heard the screams of our wives and women and children, they -- then the groups were brought together. And from then on we continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if -- in saying that nothing was taken away from you when you were searched?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. I already said in my statement that at that moment nothing was taken from us. However, as we passed the border, we gave some money to a person. I have described this also in my testimony in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that. Earlier today you said that you had decided to leave Donja Stubla because you felt unsafe because the Serbian forces were around and you feared that they would come in and slaughter you and you were also short of food. And on page 4, paragraph 4; English version page 5, paragraph 4; and Albanian 4 and 5, you said that 1.300 people including the villagers of Zegra decided to go to Macedonia because you were left without food, and you decided to go to Macedonia also and that you were afraid. Am I right in saying that once you decided to leave there were no forces in your village, neither the police nor the military?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: It's true that there were no army or police in Stublla; however, around the area in some other villages around, there were forces of the army and the police. At the moment we left there was nobody there; however, we always felt scared. We thought that they would come one day and slaughter us all in the village of Stublla.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But these forces had been in the same place for the previous five weeks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Which forces are you talking about? Five weeks I stayed with my family in the Stublla. These forces were around us. During all the time the conflict went on until when NATO intervened, these forces were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. You said that the conflict went on. What were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I was talking about the war in Kosova. During that time, the army was there, the military were there, the paramilitary were there, and they did all kind of things against the civilian population. I'm talking about that time. They were in permanent action during that time. People suffered a lot in their hands. Everybody saw them. There were murders, maltreatment, beatings, imprisonment until the last days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, you said that you had spent five weeks in the village of Donja Stubla. My question was, During that time, were Serbian forces in the area around Stubla while you were there? Were they there the whole time?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: They were in the surroundings of Stublla. The distance of 5, 6 kilometres away from the village, it's there where these forces were present. They were there all the time. However, they were not in Stublla. They did not come there for as long as we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you worked as a teacher until 2001, and you also said that you had graduated from the Faculty of Technology. When did you graduate, in which year?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I graduated from the Faculty of Technology in 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And at what university?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The University of Kosova -- there was only one university in Kosova at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I heard that this was in Pristina? Did you say that? or maybe I misheard.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes. Once it was in Prishtina, then it was transferred to Mitrovica; however, it was the same university, the University of Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You started working as a teacher in 1974. Which subject did you teach?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I taught physics, and also I taught subjects in which I was needed to teach the subjects the school asked me to teach depending on its needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who did you receive your salary from?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: At that time I received the salary from the state which existed at that time in Kosova, from the Government of Kosova, from the Yugoslav Federation which existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where did you teach, in which institution?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: As I told you earlier, in the elementary school of Zhegra as well as in the gymnasium of Gjilan. That gymnasium had some classes in Zhegra at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in 1999?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: In 1999, at that time I was in charge of collecting financial means for the Government of Kosova. That money was used to pay for the teachers, for the education which was separated at that time from Serbia. The wages of the teachers at the time were not paid by the state. This started to happen from 1999 -- 1990, 9-0. So from that time when the autonomy was abolished, all the money for the educational sector were paid by the people of Kosova themselves. So at that time I was responsible for collecting the money from the citizens for the Government of Kosova for the institutions of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me first, according to which syllabus did you teach in 1999?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The syllabus of that time was drawn up by the so-called Republic of Kosova. At that time we did not have a state, but, as I told you, the education was separated. This was imposed on us actually. The Serbs tried to force us to be taught only in Serbian language. They also sought to eliminate many Albanian-language subjects. They ordered that the subjects should be taught in Serbian language. So this led to the separation of the education. The autonomy of Kosova was lifted and at that time the process of the separation of us from the state of Serbia began to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us twice that the autonomy was abolished. Can you tell us how you understood this abolishing of autonomy, what did it mean to you personally?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The abolition of autonomy was a deprivation of the elementary rights of people of Kosova. This was taken us -- taken away from us forcefully from Serbia. They used all kinds of violence to abolish the autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell me that the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija had a different position and status from the one enjoyed by the autonomous province of Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The status at that time was the same; however, the status of Kosova was abolished. The delegates in the Assembly of Kosova on 2nd of July declared Kosova a republic. These were the delegates elected by the people. They rejected the violence of Serbia. This was the declaration of 2nd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What Assembly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Assembly of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who was the president of the Assembly of Kosovo, or are you referring to the parallel Assembly that was set up solely by the Albanian ethnic community? Is that what you were referring to? Or are you referring to the socialist, or rather, the Assembly of the socialist autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The Assembly of autonomous province, the Assembly is the parliament of Kosova. On 2nd of July they declared Kosova a republic. The majority of deputies took this decision. That was also the decision of the citizens of Kosova. Since Serbia was imposing violent measures, they led to that situation. The violent measures in Kosova continued to be applied until 12th of June, 1999. There were also different kinds of repression.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said "the government" you were referring to the government of Mr. Bukoshi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: This government you're talking about was set up in exile. The Assembly of Kosova was legitimate. It was that Assembly who declared the Republic of Kosova. At that time, on 7th of September, the Constitution of Kosova was drafted. Then due to the repression of the Serbs, all these deputies were forced to go into exile.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the so-called Kacanik constitution?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I'm talking about the Kacanik constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When were you collecting the money that you mentioned, the funds that were intended for education?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Are you talking about the date? The year?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the period in which you did this.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I was a member of a commission since this fund was set up, then as a collector of the means, I worked from -- for two years, from 1997 until 1999, so from 1997 until 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the Kosovo Liberation Army is?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was the Kosovo Liberation Army involved in?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: From its title itself you can understand that this was an armed formation who put itself in the service of the liberation of Kosova from the military and paramilitary Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the first time you heard or learned some information about the liberation -- Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: As soon as it came out in public. I learnt about it from the media. I had no idea about its existence before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what did you know about their activities?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I do not know anything about their actions. It was their business. I was engaged in my own business. At that time, I was working as a citizen to collect the money for the compensation. I was collecting the money for the teachers as well as for the health people. This was the activity I was dedicating myself to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Don't you think that this period between 1997 and 1999 while you were raising funds actually coincides with the period when, as you put it, the KLA came into public and announced what its activities were.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: The fund existed even before the KLA existed. Soon after the autonomy was abolished, the fund came into being. And it was from that time that the fund has been working on. The purpose of the fund was purely humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Based on what can you claim that the KLA was not present in Zegra before the war or immediately after the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I never heard about any action of KLA in the village of Zhegra or its surroundings. Even in Gjilan, I never heard about them doing anything in Gjilan. Actually, there's been no KLA there. I've also mentioned this in my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's precisely why I'm asking you this. How do you perceive someone to be a member of the KLA? How can you make this distinction and say, Yes, this man is a member of KLA; or no, he is not?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: It's easy to make that distinction based on the practical actions of a person. If a person belongs to an armed formation, he of course acts to obey to the orders given by that formation. He has his uniform and then he also is engaged in fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, we have heard a number of witnesses here who told us that they were members of the KLA but were dressed in civilian clothes, and they told us also that they took part in some armed actions and some other activities as well. However, you believe that only persons in uniforms were members of the KLA and that led you to tell us that there were no KLA presence in your village.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I can tell you only this: There were no KLA people in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the fact that there were people in your village in illegal possession of fire-arms?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: I did not see anybody carrying such weapons; however, during the war if anybody had such weapons, they just hid them away. They were not able to use them. I know of no case of anybody having any fire-arm with him at that moment in Zhegra or in other places. Could you be more specific about the time-frame you're asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, my question was: Before the war, prior to 1999, you aware that certain villagers had fire-arms in possession illegally, they were not bearing those arms, they were just keeping them. And I also want to ask you if you know if any lawsuits were instigated against them?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI
utterances.text: As far as I know, before 1999 the police in Zhegra, in Gjilan, in Kosova, mounted an action to collect weapons from the civilians, from the citizens. Many people were subjected to maltreatment at that time. Even people who had no weapons, sometimes they were subjected to maltreatment. This action continued. It started from the time when the autonomy was lifted. The purpose was to disarm the Albanians of any weapons they had. It was a police action. It was a notorious action of Serbian police of Yugoslavia. These were the forces which operated in Kosova. There were widespread maltreatments. Some people also died during the torture.
